claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature loading.
The improvement in plastic strain and toughness is primarily caused by edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Plastic flow in pure tungsten is dominated by less-mobile screw dislocations.
Multi-element mixing in WTaTiVZr produces severe lattice distortions.
Local lattice strains lower the activation barrier for edge-dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Edge dislocations accommodate deformation more uniformly than screw dislocations and thereby delay crack initiation.
The initial HEA is equimolar WTaTiVZr.
The WTaTiVZr HEA has a BCC structure.
The HEA and tungsten specimens should have comparable grain size and texture.
Temperatures of 800–1000 °C are relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service.
Under service-relevant high-temperature loading, severe lattice distortion produces a dense network of mobile edge dislocations in WTaTiVZr.
The HEA will exhibit lower creep displacement than pure tungsten.
The HEA will exhibit a higher activation energy for plastic flow than pure tungsten.
The HEA will exhibit a greater prevalence of edge-dislocation activity than pure tungsten.
Greater edge-dislocation activity will correlate with enhanced plastic strain and toughness in the HEA.
Pure tungsten will have lower plastic-deformation capacity and higher creep displacement than the HEA under identical conditions.
Grain-boundary phases or precipitates may supersede the proposed dislocation mechanism.
The proposed mechanism may be less applicable at lower temperatures because thermal activation is diminished.
A statistically significant absence of increased edge-dislocation density or of improved creep resistance and toughness relative to tungsten would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says lattice strain lowers the activation barrier for edge-dislocation nucleation and mobility, whereas the prediction calls for a higher activation energy for plastic flow. No distinction between the edge-dislocation barrier and the measured macroscopic activation energy is provided.

More-mobile edge dislocations are said to facilitate plastic flow, but the HEA is also predicted to have lower creep displacement than tungsten. Enhanced ductility and creep resistance can coexist, but the hypothesis does not explain how increased dislocation mobility produces reduced time-dependent deformation.
